newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: US seeks negotiations on mines, fissile material.
newsitem.headline: US seeks negotiations on mines, fissile material.

text.p: The United States lost its latest bid on Tuesday to get the United Nations-sponsored Conference on Disarmament (CD) to start work on a global ban on landmines.

Katharine Crittenberger, acting head of the U.S. delegation, expressed regret that the 61-member body was unable to take a decision on a stalled Western proposal to name a special coordinator on landmines.
But she said that Washington hoped the move could be taken on Thursday -- the last day of the current session.

The appointee would seek consensus at the Geneva talks to launch negotiations on a global accord which would ban the use, storage, production and transfer of landmines. The weapons are blamed for causing 25,000 deaths a year, mainly civilians.
"I hope we will be in a position to take a positive decision on Thursday," Crittenberger said after Sri Lanka's ambassador asked for more time to get voting instructions from his capital.
But the body looks set to return for its last seven-week round on July 28 without having reached consensus on a special coordinator or on its 1997 work programme, diplomats said.
Cuba and Syria, supported by Burma and Morocco, are holding up progress on landmines by linking the issue to their demands for an overall package including nuclear disarmament, they added.
Mexico, under heavy diplomatic pressure from the United States, announced last Thursday that it favoured starting talks on landmines if the ultimate aim was negotiating a total ban.
"The Mexicans are on board now," one senior envoy told Reuters. "But Syria and Cuba are definitely not. Burma and Morocco also still want a package."
Non-aligned countries including India and Cuba have tabled a work programme which would set up a committee to work for total elimination of nuclear weapons within a fixed period.
But the five declared nuclear weapon states -- Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States -- categorically reject such demands for negotiations in Geneva on total disarmament.
They argue the best way is for Washington and Moscow to continue taking bilateral steps to reduce their nuclear stocks.
"In regard to nuclear arms, bilateral negotiations work," Crittenberger said in her speech on Tuesday. "They have succeeded in the past and they remain intensely needed now.
"The Conference on Disarmament is not the appropriate forum to pursue agreements to reduce nuclear arsenals -- at least not at this stage," the U.S. delegate added.
She repeated a U.S. call for launching negotiations to halt production of bomb- making fissile material (plutonium and highly-enriched uranium) as the next step in the nuclear arena.
"All those who consider nuclear disarmament a priority for the CD should look upon the negotiation of a Fissile Material Cut-off Treaty as an important and positive step," she said.
"This in practice would place an upper limit on the amount of fissile material that can ever be used for nuclear weapons."

In her speech, Crittenberger backed work on landmines in the Geneva forum, which unlike Canada's "Ottawa Process" includes China and Russia, both major users and producers. Belgium is hosting four-day talks from Tuesday under Canada's initiative which aims to clinch the first anti-mine treaty in December.
But Sri Lanka took the floor in the special public plenary to say it could not yet endorse naming a special coordinator.

Maria Krasnohorska, Slovakia's ambassador who serves as chairwoman, said: "I call on the delegations to do their utmost to enable the Conference to decide on the Crittenberger said that the talks remained "just as deadlocked" as at the start of the 1997 session on January 21.
"The CD has not yet been able to carry out significant substantive work this year...In the ultimate analysis, we are not here to debate, we are here to negotiate," she said.
